subject: literature
passage: "Ulysses," a poem by Alfred Tennyson published in 1842, is spoken by the hero of Homer's Odyssey years after his return home. Now an aging king, he looks back on his voyages and ahead to what remains of his life. Readers often take the poem as a celebration of restless adventure, but its view of age is more exacting than that. The speaker treats old age not as a time of rest that has been earned, but as a time that still demands worthwhile labor: being old, in his view, does not excuse a man from the obligation to accomplish something before he dies.
stem: Which quotation from "Ulysses" most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: "Tho' much is taken, much abides; and tho' / We are not now that strength which in old days / Moved earth and heaven, that which we are, we are;"
choices.B: "This is my son, mine own Telemachus, / To whom I leave the sceptre and the isle,"
choices.C: "I am a part of all that I have met; / Yet all experience is an arch wherethro' / Gleams that untravell'd world whose margin fades / For ever and for ever when I move."
choices.D: "Old age hath yet his honour and his toil; / Death closes all: but something ere the end, / Some work of noble note, may yet be done,"

explanation.why: The claim is specific: old age still demands worthwhile labor, and being old does not excuse a man from accomplishing something. The quotation must link old age with work still owed. Only the lines that give old age "his toil" and insist that "some work of noble note, may yet be done" before death say this.
explanation.A: Incorrect. These lines admit lost strength and affirm that the speaker's identity endures, but they say nothing about work still to be done; they express persistence, not obligation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. These lines hand over the kingdom to the speaker's son and concern his departure, not the demands of old age.
explanation.C: Incorrect. These lines express the speaker's hunger for new experience, not the idea that old age carries an obligation to labor.
explanation.D: Correct. The lines assign old age its own "toil" and insist that "some work of noble note" remains to be done before death, which is the claim exactly.
